raw.quick_summary: Recursive factorial evaluation descends from n to the base case 0, then returns results upward through suspended caller frames. The base case is what stops further recursive calls; without it, each call requests a smaller argument indefinitely, so the computation does not terminate and the call stack keeps growing.

key_concepts.explanation: Factorial is defined by f(0)=1 and, for positive n, f(n)=n*f(n-1).
The rule f(0)=1 terminates the downward recursive descent and supplies the first result for unwinding.
For n=3, calls are made in the order 3, 2, 1, 0 before any suspended caller can finish.
Suspended recursive callers are stored in last-in-first-out order while waiting for their child call to return.
After f(0) returns 1, suspended calls resume in reverse order and produce 1, 2, and finally 6.
If the base case is removed, every call continues by requesting f(n-1), so there is no return point and the stack continues to accumulate frames.

visual_flow.reason: The material centers on a clear ordered process: recursive calls descend to a stopping condition, then suspended frames unwind to produce the result. A second branch shows that removing the stopping condition causes unbounded descent.

learning_path.title: How Recursive Factorial Terminates
learning_path.reason: The lesson follows the actual execution structure: definition, descent, stopping point, unwinding, and failure without a base case.

steps.title: Identify the two factorial rules
steps.learning_goal: Distinguish the base case from the recursive case.
steps.explanation: Factorial has a stopping rule, f(0)=1, and a recursive rule, f(n)=n*f(n-1) for positive n. Both are needed for a complete computation.
steps.connection_to_previous: This establishes the rules that govern every later call.

steps.title: Trace the downward calls
steps.learning_goal: Follow the order in which recursive calls are created.
steps.explanation: Starting with f(3), the computation requests f(2), then f(1), then f(0). The callers cannot finish yet because each is waiting for its child result.
steps.connection_to_previous: The recursive rule explains why each positive argument creates the next smaller call.

steps.title: Use the base case to stop descent
steps.learning_goal: Explain why f(0)=1 is the termination point.
steps.explanation: At f(0), the base-case rule applies instead of making another recursive call. It returns 1, giving the waiting computation a result to use.
steps.connection_to_previous: The descent is safe only because it eventually reaches this explicitly defined stopping rule.

steps.title: Unwind the suspended frames
steps.explanation: The f(1) frame resumes first and returns 1, then f(2) returns 2, and finally f(3) returns 6. This reverse order reflects the call stack’s last-in-first-out organization.
steps.connection_to_previous: The base-case result travels back through the suspended callers created during descent.

steps.title: Analyze the missing-base-case failure
steps.explanation: If f(0)=1 is removed, no call has permission to stop. Each call continues to request a smaller argument, so no result returns and pending frames keep accumulating on the stack.
steps.connection_to_previous: Comparing this branch with the normal trace reveals that termination depends on the base case, not merely on making the argument smaller.

checkpoint_questions.question: What role does f(0)=1 play in the computation of f(3)?

options.text: It starts another recursive call with argument -1.
It stops descent and supplies the first result for unwinding.
It stores every pending caller in the stack.
It multiplies all arguments at once.

checkpoint_questions.explanation: The base case both stops further calls and returns the value that lets suspended callers resume.

checkpoint_questions.question: Why are the intermediate results returned in the order 1, 1, 2, 6?

options.text: The caller frames finish in the same order they were created.
The deepest call returns first, then suspended callers resume in last-in-first-out order.
The multiplication rule reverses the call order before any return.

checkpoint_questions.explanation: f(0) returns first; then f(1), f(2), and f(3) resume as the stack unwinds.

checkpoint_questions.question: What happens if the base case is removed?

options.text: The calls continue requesting smaller arguments, so no result returns and the stack grows.
The stack automatically skips to f(0).
The recursive rule becomes iterative and terminates.

checkpoint_questions.explanation: Without a stopping rule, every call makes another recursive call; the process does not terminate.
